parts.label: (a)
key_concepts: atomic mass unit to MeV conversion
hints: Hint 1: Think about which fundamental principle links mass directly to energy, and identify the mass of $1.00\text{ u}$ in $\text{kg}$ and the speed of light you will need.
Hint 2: Calculate the energy in joules first, then convert joules to electronvolts using $1\text{ eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$ and express the result in MeV.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link mass to energy**
You are sitting with a tiny mass, $1.00\text{ u}$, and you want its energy equivalent. Mass and energy are the same thing in different forms, linked by Einstein's relation. In SI units $1\text{ u} = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$ and $c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Calculate and convert to MeV**
First find energy in joules: $$E = mc^2 = (1.66 \times 10^{-27}) \times (3.0 \times 10^8)^2 = 1.49 \times 10^{-10}\text{ J}$$ Then convert to eV by dividing by $1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J eV}^{-1}$: $$E = \frac{1.49 \times 10^{-10}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}} = 9.34 \times 10^8\text{ eV} = 934\text{ MeV}$$ This is why mass defect in u multiplied by 934 gives binding energy in MeV.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 12.1 for $^{235}$U and remind yourself what mass defect means - the mass lost when separate nucleons bind together, which appears as binding energy.
Hint 2: Convert the mass defect in u to total binding energy in MeV using the result from (a), then share that energy equally among all 235 nucleons.
parts.proper_answer: Total binding energy $= 1.865 \times 934 = 1742\text{ MeV}$. Binding energy per nucleon $= 1742/235 = 7.41\text{ MeV}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **From mass defect to total binding energy**
For $^{235}_{92}$U the table gives mass defect $= 1.865\text{ u}$. That missing mass has become the energy holding the nucleus together. Using $1\text{ u} = 934\text{ MeV}$: $$E_B = 1.865 \times 934 = 1742\text{ MeV}$$ This is the energy you would need to pull all 235 nucleons completely apart.

Step 2: **Divide by nucleon number**
Binding energy per nucleon measures stability per particle: $$E_B \text{ per nucleon} = \frac{E_B}{A} = \frac{1741.9}{235} = 7.41\text{ MeV}$$ So complete Fig. 12.1 with $7.41\text{ MeV}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Recall the shape of the binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number curve, which peaks near iron and falls slowly for very heavy nuclei like uranium.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the BE per nucleon curve**
Binding energy per nucleon rises to a maximum around $A \approx 56$ (iron) and then gradually decreases for heavier nuclei because long-range Coulomb repulsion between many protons offsets the short-range strong force. Rutherfordium with $A = 267$ is heavier than uranium with $A = 235$, so it lies further down the falling tail. Hence its binding energy per nucleon is less.

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Think about why fission releases energy - the two lighter product nuclei are more tightly bound per nucleon than the heavy parent, so extra binding energy is given out.
Hint 2: Find the change in mass defect or the change in total binding energy between products (Mo + La) and reactant (U) and convert to MeV.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Energy from extra binding**
In fission the total binding energy increases. The released energy equals binding energy of products minus binding energy of reactant. Equivalently it equals increase in mass defect times 934.

Step 2: **Insert the table values**
Mass defect increase: $$\Delta m = (0.859 + 1.219) - 1.865 = 0.213\text{ u}$$ Convert to energy: $$E = 0.213 \times 934 = 199\text{ MeV}$$ The same result follows from $(95 \times 8.443 + 139 \times 8.189) - (235 \times 7.41)$. About $199\text{ MeV}$ per fission is released as kinetic energy of products and radiation.

parts.label: (d)
hints: Hint 1: Start from the amount in moles and think how to get the actual number of uranium nuclei that fission - each nucleus gives one reaction.
Hint 2: Recall how to change the energy per reaction from MeV to joules in SI units for a power calculation.
Hint 3: Combine total energy from all reactions with the short time interval using power equals total energy divided by time.
parts.proper_answer: Number $= 1.2 \times 10^{-7} \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 7.22 \times 10^{16}$. Energy per fission $= 199 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-13} = 3.18 \times 10^{-11}\text{ J}$. Power $= 7.22 \times 10^{16} \times 3.18 \times 10^{-11} / (25 \times 10^{-3}) = 9.2 \times 10^7\text{ W}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Count the fissions**
Moles tells you how many particles you have. With Avogadro constant $N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}$: $$N = nN_A = (1.2 \times 10^{-7}) \times (6.02 \times 10^{23}) = 7.22 \times 10^{16}$$ Each $^{235}$U nucleus undergoes one reaction, so this is the number of reactions.

Step 2: **Energy per reaction in joules**
From (c) one reaction gives $199\text{ MeV}$. Since $1\text{ MeV} = 10^6 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J} = 1.60 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$: $$E_1 = 199 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-13} = 3.18 \times 10^{-11}\text{ J}$$

Step 3: **Total energy to average power**
Total energy is number times energy per reaction. Average power is total energy divided by time $t = 25\text{ ms} = 25 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}$: $$P = \frac{N E_1}{t} = \frac{7.22 \times 10^{16} \times 3.18 \times 10^{-11}}{25 \times 10^{-3}} = 9.2 \times 10^7\text{ W}$$ This huge power from a tiny mass shows why nuclear energy is so concentrated.
